title: Ben Shelton’s window of French Open opportunity closes with second-round upset loss
content:
PARIS — Ben Shelton’s window of French Open opportunity has closed.

For a few hours Thursday, Shelton was the favorite to reach the men’s final on his side of the draw.

Jannik Sinner had lost. So too had Daniil Medvedev. Felix Auger-Aliassime has had little recent success on clay or at the French Open.

There was Shelton, the No. 5 seed, with a seemingly winnable match against Raphaël Collignon of Belgium, the world No. 62. Collignon has been to the third round of a major just once in his career. Shelton, meanwhile, has been to two Grand Slam semifinals. He is a player who loves the big stage and knows an opportunity when he sees one.

As night fell on Paris, whatever vision Shelton may have had for the rest of his fortnight went by the wayside, in an endless flurry of nearly flawless tennis from Collignon that produced a 6-4, 7-5, 6-4 win.

Collignon had Shelton off balance and on the defensive all night. He pelted returns — sometimes high, sometimes on a wire over the net. He was the more creative player, dictating points the way Shelton usually does.

Shelton won just 69 percent of points on his first serve, which is his bread and butter. Collignon won 88 percent of his first serve points, which is nearly untouchable by his standards. On average, he hit his first serve harder than Shelton’s, averaging 126 mph compared with 118 for Shelton. It was on return, with Shelton winning just 18 percent of the points he played and failing to create a single break point, that the match was lost. Collignon earned six break points and converted three — one per set. That was more than enough.

The effort, one of the best of Collignon’s career, left him in tears at mid-court after he rolled a backhand into the corner off a sloppy Shelton drop shot.

For Shelton, the loss was a disappointing end to a European clay-court swing that started with so much promise. He won the Munich Open, at the time the biggest title for an American man in Europe in more than two decades, before losing early at three consecutive events, including the two ATP Masters 1000 Madrid and Italian Opens.

He arrived in Paris hoping that his past success at Grand Slams would translate into confidence and proficiency. He got off to a good start, winning his opening match in 100 minutes.

He was done Thursday night almost as quickly, in just a minute over two hours, and Collingnon was off to the third round in what is now a wide-open side of the draw.
